<reason>Side A dismantled the proposition by showing how regulating unpredictable third-party human behavior differs from disclosing static physical defects like lead paint. When Side B defined the trigger around "management logs" and later proposed a "six-month incident-free" window, Side A proved both mechanisms backfire: logging triggers punish proactive landlords who track complaints while rewarding slumlords who keep no records, and rolling windows cannot stop risk-averse landlords from attaching permanent, useless boilerplate disclaimers to every lease. Worse, Side B twice confused the two sides' worlds (in B3.1 and B5.2), arguing that Side A's regime punishes diligent landlords with a "scarlet letter" when only Side B's mandate creates that disclosure penalty in the first place.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [A4.1] and [A5.1], Side A lethally turned Side B's own phrasing from [B3.1] and [B5.2] against the motion, pointing out that without a disclosure mandate there is no "scarlet letter" for keeping maintenance logs—meaning Side B had accidentally described the exact perverse incentive created by its own rule.</best_rebuttal>
